messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Threat → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kofi's eyes still scan the room with an intensity that makes his wife, Ama, worry. It's been two years since the incident with the police, but the way he flinches at every sudden noise, the way his shoulders tense when a stranger approaches him on the street – it's as if his body has learned to expect danger around every corner. As a curriculum designer, Kofi spends most of his days in front of a computer screen, but even the familiar hum of the office can't calm the hypervigilance that has become second nature to him. When memories of that night resurface – and they do, often without warning – Kofi feels like he's drowning. He'll be working on a project, lost in thought, when suddenly the sound of sirens or the smell of asphalt will transport him back to the scene: his hands cuffed behind his back, the officer's knee pressing into his spine, the feeling of helplessness that threatened to consume him. It's not just the image that overwhelms him – it's the emotions that come flooding back, unbidden and intense. Kofi has tried to put the experience into words for Ama, but every time he attempts to recount what happened, he finds himself stuck on a single, searing detail: the look in the officer's eyes. Sometimes, the memories come without any clear image at all – just a wave of anxiety that crashes over him, leaving Kofi breathless and disoriented. It's as if his body remembers the trauma even when his mind can't quite grasp it. When this happens, Ama tries to be patient, but she can see the fear in her husband's eyes, the way he struggles to ground himself in the present moment. She knows that Kofi is trying to make sense of what happened, to find a way to process the emotions and memories that still haunt him. As time has passed, Kofi has become more adept at avoiding triggers – no news programs or cop dramas for him – but it's hard to avoid the world entirely. And when he does venture out, his hypervigilance is always on high alert, scanning for potential threats. It's exhausting, and Ama worries that one day he'll just shut down completely. The other night, Kofi had a nightmare so intense that he woke up drenched in sweat, his heart racing like it used to when the police first approached him. That's what finally brought him to seek help – the realization that two years on, the memories still have the power to consume him whole. Kofi is afraid of losing himself completely, of becoming a shadow of the man he once was. He hopes that therapy will give him back some sense of control over his life, over his memories and emotions. For now, though, the past remains a raw, open wound – one that still has the power to startle him awake in the dead of night.
